Li Kwai-wah also said that the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (the Alliance) "used human rights as a shield" to organise public activities that stirred up emotions, colluded with external forces, and when public sentiment was cooling, "added new elements to boost the number of participants," which Li said were characteristics of incitement.

Li Kwai-wah then cited the judgment, pointing out that Chow Hang-tung admitted in court that by drawing parallels between the anti-extradition bill events and the Tiananmen Square crackdown, she helped promote the idea of incitement to subvert state power. He also said it was an indisputable fact that the Alliance had, year after year, sown seeds of hatred toward the Chinese Communist Party and the central government, adding that the ruling would assist future law enforcement.

Li Kwai-wah said there is a difference between criticism and acts of incitement and subversion, which he noted the national security law has already made clear. He also said each case must be handled on its own merits and one cannot generalise, adding that the ruling was "well-reasoned and well-supported," and "also lets the public know that it is not that one cannot criticise or do certain things; it is simply that there must absolutely not be any incitement, absolutely not any subversion of state power."

Li Kwai-wah said whether public mourning is allowed depends on its nature

When asked whether anyone openly mourning the Tiananmen Square crackdown in the future would be breaking the law, and given that the ruling pointed out there is no possibility of Western-style party rotation under Chinese Communist Party rule, whether he was concerned the court might be seen by Western countries as认定 China an authoritarian state, thereby affecting Hong Kong's international image.

Will openly mourning the Tiananmen Square crackdown be illegal?

Li Kwai-wah first responded by saying, "I don't see the word 'authoritarian,' so don't add things into it yourself." He then said every country has its own system, and what is happening now is precisely the execution of our own system to a high standard, "in English it is prescribed by law, you can look it up." As for whether openly mourning the Tiananmen Square crackdown in the future would be illegal, Li said one cannot generalise, and a decision can only be made based on the specifics. He also pointed out that if an activity is related to a public event, one must comply with the Public Order Ordinance, the National Security Law, the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, and other relevant legislation, and the police will take the provisions into account when processing applications.

CE: Alliance sowed seeds of hatred toward the centre. Chief Executive John Lee responded to the ruling by saying that the Alliance had, over a long period, deliberately sown seeds of hatred toward the Chinese Communist Party and the central government within Hong Kong society, using various means to attempt to provoke citizens' feelings of disgust and hatred toward the Chinese Communist Party and the central government, and to incite the masses to subvert state power.

He said the defendants' long-standing behaviour had endangered national security, their conspiracy was clear for all to see, and they must be punished. A government statement also said the Alliance's fundamental proposition and objective was to end the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party and overturn the Constitution of the People's Republic of China, adding that the court's ruling was delivered with forceful and measured reasoning.

The Toronto Alliance said the evidence against Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan was that they advocated "ending one-party dictatorship," which has been one of the Alliance's five major platforms since its founding in 1989. Toronto Alliance co-chair Wu Wen-wen (Nora Wu) said, "What crime is there in demanding an end to one-party dictatorship!" She said it was no different from the democratic demands put forward by the 1989 Tiananmen Square student movement.

Toronto Alliance vice-chair Li Lan-ju said: "Lee Cheuk-yan devoted his life to pursuing equality for Hong Kong and China, and convicting him of 'incitement to subvert state power' is a grave insult to him." Li Lan-ju was one of the student union members who went to Beijing in 1989.

Amnesty International Hong Kong Overseas Section spokesperson Zhang Chao-xiong (Fernando Cheung) said the ruling was heartbreaking and once again proved that the Hong Kong National Security Law is being used to punish those who peacefully mourn the Tiananmen Square crackdown.
